source.version: Completed Research Paper for the Forty-Sixth International Conference on Information Systems, Nashville, Tennessee, USA 2025, as printed on p. 1 and the page footers. No revision date or version number is printed.
source.title_on_document: When AI Joins the Brainstorm: Impacts of Generative Language Models on Collaborative Divergent Thinking

paper_design_summary: Bachelor-level students generated ideas for their course digital-innovation projects in self-organized groups assigned to live or round-based collaboration, with or without a GPT-4o AI peer that supplied ideas during brainstorming (pp. 4-5, Study design and Workshop Session). The paper reports a research sample of 96 students and scores participant fluency, idea elaboration, and originality; it also compares AI-generated and human-generated ideas within this same experiment (pp. 6-8; p. 14, Conclusion).

studies.label: Course-project brainstorming: collaboration structure by AI-peer presence

assignment.what_was_assigned: Student groups were assigned to four conditions crossing live versus round-based idea sharing with AI-peer presence versus absence. The paper calls the experiment randomized but does not describe the randomization procedure. Each condition occupied a separate classroom (p. 4, Study design; p. 5, Workshop Session).
assignment.quote: We conducted a randomized controlled experiment (N=96) with four conditions
assignment.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Study design; p. 5, Workshop Session (group assignment and four conditions)
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is identified in the document (pp. 1-17).

arms.name: Live
arms.description: Live collaboration without an AI peer; human group members see ideas in real time (p. 4, Intervention Design; p. 5, Workshop Session).

arms.name: Rounds
arms.description: Round-based collaboration without an AI peer; ideas from preceding rounds are shared with human group members (pp. 4-5, Intervention Design and Workshop Session).

arms.name: Live AI
arms.description: Live collaboration with an AI peer automatically contributing one new idea whenever users submit three ideas (p. 4, Intervention Design; p. 5, Workshop Session).

arms.name: Rounds AI
arms.description: Round-based collaboration with an AI peer generating two ideas per round; ideas from preceding rounds are shown to participants (p. 4, Intervention Design; p. 5, Workshop Session).

participants.exclusions: The course involved 108 students; 96 consented to research, and no data were collected from nonconsenting students (p. 4, Participants). The reported research sample of 96 is recorded as analyzed, supported by the experiment N in the abstract, the conclusion, and the statement that all participants were pooled; separate outcome-specific participant denominators and arm counts are not given (p. 1; p. 14, Limitations and Conclusion). No additional person-level exclusions are stated. Ideas rated irrelevant (relevance score of 1 by either rater) and non-idea contributions were removed, leaving 582 ideas (p. 6, analysis preamble). The unfiltered rating pool contained 680 ideas (p. 7, Ideas’ Originality); the retained pool contained 426 human-generated and 156 AI-generated ideas (p. 8). The questionnaire section reports 99 responses and 63 retained qualitative responses, inconsistent with the stated consenting sample; these response counts are not used as participant counts (p. 10, User Experience).
participants.who: Bachelor-level students in economics, data science, or sports and economics taking an information systems design course. The course used self-organized groups of up to five members; the paper reports 23 groups (p. 4, Participants; p. 14, Conclusion).
participants.country: Switzerland (p. 14, Limitations: one class at a Swiss university)
participants.quote: Our experiment with 96 students across 23 groups revealed several key contributions.
participants.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Participants; p. 14, Limitations and Conclusion; p. 10, User Experience (inconsistent response count)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4o (p. 4, Intervention Design; p. 16, OpenAI reference)
ai_tool.how_used: An AI peer embedded in the Graasp ideation-board application automatically supplied ideas during the task. Its prompt contained the group problem statement, participants’ ideas, and instructions to generate a new idea. AI contributions were marked as AI-generated; the AI could initiate ideas but could not build on another idea. Supply was two ideas per round in Rounds AI and one per three user submissions in Live AI (p. 4, Intervention Design).

task.description: Generate short, anonymous ideas for a digital-innovation prototype addressing a group-selected challenge aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Ideas were limited to 200 characters. Participants could append contributions to existing ideas; a voting phase followed brainstorming (pp. 4-5, Intervention Design and Workshop Session).
task.duration: A nominal 15-minute ideation phase followed by 5 minutes of voting, within a 2-hour workshop in week 6 of the course (p. 5, Workshop Session). Actual ideation duration varied; fluency was normalized to ideas per 15 minutes (pp. 6-7, Participant’s Creative Fluency).

outcomes.name: Participant creative fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas generated by each participant, normalized by the group’s actual activity duration to ideas per 15 minutes. Bayesian negative-binomial model; analysis unit is the individual, with no group-level or multilevel model (pp. 6-7, Participant’s Creative Fluency, equations 1-2 and Figure 1). The printed intervals are 94% Bayesian highest-density intervals (HDIs); the confidence_interval flag denotes availability of an interval, not a frequentist confidence interval. The paper labels the effects d_agent and d_collaboration without specifying their standardizing denominator.

outcomes.name: Elaboration of participants’ ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Deterministic word-count score after removing stopwords with NLTK and its stopword corpus; automated_score here denotes this computed length score. Bayesian normal model at the idea level, without participant or group clustering (p. 6, analysis-level description; p. 7, Participants Elaboration, equation 3). An elaboration-specific number of analyzed ideas is not printed. Reported intervals are 94% Bayesian HDIs; the standardizer for the printed d_agent effects is not defined.

outcomes.name: Originality of human-generated ideas (human ratings and OCSAI)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two independent human raters scored originality on a seven-point scale; the paper also used the Open Creativity Scoring with Artificial Intelligence (OCSAI) model, fine-tuned on human-rated divergent-thinking responses. Originality was normalized to 0-1. The human-rater mean and OCSAI were compared in Figure 3 (pp. 7-8, Ideas’ Originality). These measurement variants are kept in one outcome. The measure field records a confirmed method used, but the paper does not identify which score (human mean, OCSAI, or a combination) underlies the condition effects in equation (4); the numerical effects must not be treated as confirmed human-rating effects. The Bayesian normal model uses ideas as observations without participant or group clustering (p. 6; p. 8, equation 4). The retained human-generated corpus has N = 426 ideas (p. 8); per-arm counts are absent. Reported intervals are 94% Bayesian HDIs, and the standardizing denominator for d_agent is unspecified.

contrasts.reported: d_agent = -0.17 (HDI 94%: [-0.44, 0.10]); the authors describe no significant effect.

sample_overlap.quote: This research is part of a larger project aiming to design models of collaboration supported by digital tools to support and structure efficient ideation processes

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly reports a randomized experiment and assigns student groups to AI-peer versus no-AI conditions during their ordinary coursework, supporting field_rct with team assignment (p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Study design; p. 5, Workshop Session). The reported research sample is 96 students, above the threshold of 50 people (p. 4, Participants; p. 14, Conclusion); this uses the authors’ study-level sample, not the counts of ideas or questionnaire responses, and outcome-specific people counts remain unreported. Fluency, elaboration, and originality are scored on produced ideas (pp. 6-8). AI was available during idea production, so these answer with_ai. Missing clustered uncertainty affects pooling suitability rather than these three inclusion criteria.

one_line_finding: AI-peer presence reduced human fluency in live brainstorming (d_agent = -0.61, 94% HDI [-1.22, -0.07]; p. 7, Participant’s Creative Fluency), while the reported originality effects were negative but their intervals included zero (p. 8, Ideas’ Originality).
open_questions: Confirm analyzed people per arm and per outcome: 96 is the reported consenting/experiment sample, whereas p. 10 reports 99 questionnaire responses; no participant-flow or arm-count table is given (pp. 4, 10, 14).

Explain the group denominators: p. 4 and p. 14 report 23 groups, but the time-fluency correlations use N = 10 round-based groups and N = 9 live groups (p. 6, Figure 2 and accompanying paragraph). No exclusion explanation is supplied.

Which originality score underlies equation (4), the AI-assistance effect sizes, and the descriptive AI-versus-human comparison: OCSAI, mean human ratings, or a combination? Both methods are described, but the effect paragraphs and Figure 4 do not identify the score source (pp. 7-8).

What denominator defines the reported d_agent and d_collaboration effects? Can participant- and group-aware uncertainty be obtained? The paper explicitly analyzes fluency at the individual level and originality/elaboration at the idea level without group or multilevel modeling (p. 6; p. 14, Limitations).
Confirm whether any participants overlap with the related project papers cited in Intervention Design; shared participants are neither claimed nor ruled out (p. 4).
notes: Read the entire markdown conversion, including all references; it ends at PDF p. 17, with no appendix. Checked the design, participant reporting, methods, numerical effects, and cited figures against PDF text; Figures 1-4 were also inspected in memory without creating image files. PDF and printed page numbers agree. No additional supplement or preregistration is identified. The code URL is for the ideation-board application (p. 4, Intervention Design; p. 16, La Scala 2024 reference), not a stated analysis-code release; no data URL is given. The single experiment also compares AI-generated ideas (mean 0.64, median 0.64, SD 0.12, N = 156 ideas) with human-generated ideas (mean 0.44, median 0.44, SD 0.16, N = 426 ideas), reporting Mann-Whitney U = 56620, p*** < .001 (p. 8, Ideas’ Originality and Figure 4). This descriptive source-of-output comparison is not an additional participant study or an AI-assistance contrast. The additional no-AI collaboration-structure contrast is d_collaboration = -0.79 (HDI 94%: [-1.39, -0.26]) for Rounds versus Live (p. 7); it does not answer an AI-assistance question. Relevance ratings serve as an idea-exclusion filter, with no reported treatment contrast, so they are described in the methods rather than counted as a separate usefulness outcome (pp. 6-7). Co-construction via direct descendants is a collaboration proxy compared across live versus round-based conditions, not a reported similarity/diversity measure or isolated AI-assistance contrast (pp. 8-9, Collaboration Between Participants); it is not counted among the three creativity outcomes. User-experience questionnaires are not scored creative outputs and are omitted from outcomes (pp. 9-13). There is no across-people diversity or post-AI unassisted outcome. No effect sizes, standard errors, arm sample sizes, or exclusions counts have been calculated. The standardized_effect flag preserves the paper’s printed d notation; its precise standardization remains unverified. Extraction date: 2026-10-09.
